title: Introduction to Platforms
overview: A platform provides shared services and interfaces on which applications and complementary products are built. This topic connects the internal developer platform (IDP), its architecture and adoption journey to platform thinking: enabling interactions between producers and consumers. Practise explaining both the developer experience and the engineering work behind a platform business.
big_ideas: A platform is a foundation of shared services and interfaces on which outside (and inside) parties build complementary products; you work ON a platform, USE a framework and CALL a library.
Platform engineering designs, builds and operates internal platforms so application teams get **self-service**, lower **cognitive load** and no ticket-ops.
Platform Eng, DevOps and SRE are complementary: DevOps is culture and CI/CD, SRE is reliability (SLOs, error budgets, toil), platform engineering builds the internal product (IDP, golden paths).
The IDP reference model has planes: Developer Control, Integration and Delivery, Resource, Monitoring and Logging (observability), Security, plus a Data and Model plane for AI/ML.
Build a platform like a product: start with an MVP, backend (CI/CD + IaC) before portal, measure from day one (DORA metrics, developer NPS).
Platform thinking: think **roles not markets**. A platform enables interactions between Producers and Consumers around a Seed; technology is only an enabler.

Three components make a platform business work: **Magnet** (attract and retain both roles), **Toolbox** (APIs and tools to produce and consume), **Matchmaker** (accurate matching, curation, trust, data analytics).
Platforms enable business ecosystems of externally produced complements; each business aspect maps to an engineering aspect (e.g. Toolbox = SDK and API design, Matchmaker = curation and algorithms).

sections.title: What is a software platform?
sections.summary: Two complementary definitions of a platform (foundation for third-party complements; a set of services applications are built and run on) and the kinds of platform you already use.

notes.h: What is a platform: two views

items.t: **Business view**: an extensible foundation on which others build complementary products or services
sub: supplies shared core functionality and interfaces
for internal applications and external complements

items.t: **Engineering view**: provides services on which applications are built and run
sub: combines reusable application capabilities with hosting infrastructure
so it must handle discovery, resource coordination, orchestration and usage reporting

items: **Platform**: packages reusable services and domain components behind interfaces
**Several applications** sit on top of the same platform and share them
**Application** (by contrast): one product built for its own users
**Services** → Airbnb, Uber, Grab
**Marketplace** → eBay, Amazon, Carousell
**Payment** → PayPal, Stripe, PayNow
**Social networking**
**Communication** → WhatsApp, WeChat
**Content** → YouTube, Kindle
**Software development platforms** → Linux, Android
notes.foot: The common thread: outside parties build or exchange value on top of a shared foundation.

terms.def: Extensible software foundation providing shared core services and interfaces on which others build complementary products.
Designing, building and operating platforms for application development teams to leverage.

check.q: A bank's account and payment services are used only by its own mobile app; no outside party can build on them. A colleague calls this a platform. Do you agree?

items: **Engineering definition: fits** → a set of services that applications are built and run on
**Business definition: doesn't fit** → no outside parties build complementary products through its interfaces → **no ecosystem** yet
**Lecture expects both**: internal consumption **and** external complements
a.foot: To get there the bank would need **published, extensible interfaces** that partners can build against.

check.q: A company hosts its reusable services on a shared cluster but leaves service discovery, resource coordination and usage reporting to each application team. What is missing compared with the lecture's definition of a modern platform, and why does it matter?

items: **Modern platform** = both an **application architecture** and the **infrastructure** that hosts it
**Must solve itself**: discovery, resource coordination, orchestration and usage reporting
**Left to each team** → solved differently and repeatedly → the company is **sharing components**, not offering a platform
a.foot: Taking them on makes the **platform team responsible for infrastructure**, which is the work **platform engineering** exists to do.

sections.title: Characteristics and benefits of a platform
sections.summary: What makes something a good platform and what an organisation gains by building one, illustrated with Google Pay.

items: **Composable**: discrete services and components, usable independently
**Quick and cheap to start**: easy on-ramp (quick-start guides, documentation, code samples)
**Rich user community** for sharing
**Promotes interaction** among partners
**Secure and compliant** by default
**Extensible**: enables business agility
**Up to date and data-driven**: feedback loop from collecting and analysing data
**Interoperability** with disparate systems
**Different paces of change**: intra-platform change and inter-platform change move independently, without disrupting each other
**Quicker response** to opportunities through new ways of working
**Agile governance and risk management** that still protects stakeholders
**Teams, skills and culture** re-imagined
**Data available** for decision making
**Service model fits the value chain** instead of being strictly sequential

notes.lead: The lecture's worked example, characteristic → how Google Pay shows it.
items: **Agility** → easy to embed payments in e-commerce and mobile apps
**Interaction among partners** → merchants and buyers
**Rich community** → high Android adoption
**Composable, quick to start** → setup guides, tutorials, test card suite
**Data-driven** → AI analysis of spending; ML to spot phishing and fraud

items.t: **Secure and compliant** →
sub: virtual account number instead of the real card number

notes.lead: Google Pay grew beyond its first use:
items: merchant-to-buyer card payment (the start)
peer-to-peer payment
PayNow transfers
GrabPay top-ups
expense management and promo offers
notes.foot: A platform lets new services **slot into the value chain** rather than being a fixed linear process.

terms.def: Built from discrete services and components that can be used independently.
Quick-start guides, documentation and code samples that make a platform easy and cheap to begin using.

check.q: A payments API is PCI-compliant and encrypts every transaction, but partners need three weeks of contracts and manual key exchange before their first test call, and there is no sandbox. Which platform characteristic is weakest, and what would you change?

items: **Why**: the on-ramp is slow and costly → discourages **producers and consumers** from joining
**Fix**: add **quick-start guides**, **code samples**, **self-service test credentials** and a **test card suite**, as **Google Pay** does
a.foot: **Security and compliance** should stay the default, so the **sandbox must not expose real card data**.

check.q: A platform team wants to replace its internal database and messaging stack. Dozens of partner apps call its published APIs. Which platform benefit lets the team do this without a partner release, and what would break it?

items: **Stable interfaces** → the inside evolves at its own pace without overly impacting the outside
**Breaks if** the change **leaks through the interface**, e.g. altering response fields or meanings
a.foot: Then the team needs a **new API version** and a **migration period** for partners.

check.q: A platform logs every transaction, but nobody analyses the logs and its service catalogue has not changed in two years. Which characteristic is it failing, and why is collecting data not enough?

a.lead: It is failing **stays relevant and data-driven**.
items: **Needs a feedback loop**: data **collected and then analysed** to improve the services
**Examples**: Google Pay's **analysis of spending**, **ML fraud detection**
**Logs nobody reads** support no decisions → the platform **drifts away** from what its users need

sections.title: Platform vs framework vs library
sections.summary: Three levels of reuse that are often confused, distinguished by how you relate to them.

items: **Work on** a platform
**Structure** an application with a framework
**Call** a library
notes.foot: Focus on the role each plays; size or hosting alone does not define the category.

notes.lead: The environment software is designed to run in.
items: **Services and reusable components**: provides them
**Extends features**: applications consume and expose services to external parties
**Supplies tools**: the software and hardware tools needed to run an application
**Hosted service**: typically part of one, accessed by APIs
**Data and analytics**: collects data and offers analytics to monitor and improve services

items.t: **Framework**: a reusable application skeleton
sub: supports a particular architecture or design patterns
may be one component of a platform

items.t: **Library**: reusable code that your application calls at the appropriate point
sub: you stay in control of the flow

terms.def: Pre-defined skeleton with abstract classes that guides how an application is architected.
Reusable code your application calls where needed.

check.q: Your team adopts a toolkit that supplies abstract classes, dictates how the application is structured and calls your code at points it defines. A teammate calls it a library. Do you agree?

items: **Framework** = a **predefined skeleton** that **imposes a way of architecting** the application and supports certain **design patterns**
**Library** = code **you call** from your own application at points **you choose**
a.foot: A framework **shapes the whole design** → replacing it later costs **far more** than swapping a library.

check.q: An internal team announces 'we are building a platform', but its deliverable is a downloadable code skeleton that each app team installs and runs on its own servers. Is that a platform?

items: **Framework** can be **part of** a platform but is not one

items.t: **Platform** = the **environment software runs in**:
sub: provides **hosted services** and **reusable components accessed by APIs**
lets applications **extend features** by **consuming and exposing services**

a.foot: To become a platform the team would need to **host and operate shared services**, not just distribute code.

visuals.title: Platform vs framework vs library
rows: Environment with services and components, often a hosted service via APIs
Pre-defined skeleton with abstract classes and design-pattern guidance
Reusable code invoked at the right point
Hosted services or a computing environment

sections.title: Platform engineering and its place beside DevOps and SRE
sections.summary: What platform engineering is, which pain points drove it, and how it complements DevOps and SRE.

notes.lead: The practice of designing and building toolchains and workflows that enable self-service capabilities for software engineering organisations. Its three verbs:
items: **Build** → toolchains and workflows that let dev teams move faster without bottlenecks
**Enable** → self-service so developers do not wait on ops or tickets
**Scale** → manage complexity across hundreds of teams and thousands of services consistently

notes.lead: State of Platform Engineering survey of 281 professionals:
items: **Lack of automation** and repetitive manual tasks → 49%
**No standardisation** in DevOps setups → 48%
**Developer cognitive overload** → 47%
**No self-service**, i.e. pure ticket ops → 44%

items.t: **Others cited**:

notes.h: DevOps vs SRE vs platform engineering

items.t: **DevOps** = culture and practice
**SRE** = reliability engineering (from Google)
sub: applies software engineering to ops problems
SLOs, error budgets and toil reduction

items.t: **Platform engineering** = internal product teams

notes.h: Why this matters for the course
items: **Course focus**: the platform engineering role
**Treat the platform as a product** → whose customers are internal developers

terms.def: Repetitive manual operational work that SRE and platform automation aim to reduce.
SRE reliability target and the allowed amount of unreliability before change must slow.

check.q: A company's developers wait several days for an ops ticket to be approved before they get a test database. Which pain point is this, and what is the platform engineering answer?

items: **Pain point**: no **self-service** → developers **queue on operations** for routine provisioning

**Platform engineering answer**: replace the ticket with a **self-service capability** (a **portal**, **CLI** or **workload spec**) that provisions the database through an **automated, standardised workflow**
a.foot: The platform team must then **own and maintain that automation as a product**.

check.q: A CTO says: 'We already have a DevOps culture and an SRE team, so a platform team would be redundant.' Do you agree?

items: **DevOps**: **culture** and **CI/CD** with **shared responsibility**
**SRE**: applies software engineering to **reliability** through **SLOs**, **error budgets** and **toil reduction**
**Neither** builds an **internal developer platform** that treats **developers as customers** and offers **self-service golden paths**
a.foot: If the organisation has only **a few teams and services**, though, the **scale problem** a platform team solves may not exist yet.

check.q: Thirty application teams each maintain their own copied-and-edited pipeline scripts and infrastructure code. Which pain points does this show, and what would a platform offer?

items.t: **Pain points** (three of the top drivers in the survey):
sub: **lack of automation** through repeated manual work

items: **Platform offers** a **golden path**: a supported, opinionated **pipeline and provisioning route** that every team can reuse
a.foot: **Cost**: less freedom for teams with unusual needs → the platform team has to **gather feedback** and **evolve the path**.

visuals.title: DevOps vs SRE vs Platform Engineering
rows: CI/CD pipelines, shared responsibility, mostly process
Internal developer platforms, self-service golden paths
Bridges dev and ops through culture
Originated at Google; applies software engineering to ops problems
Treats dev teams as customers; reduces cognitive load at scale

sections.title: Platform engineering vocabulary
sections.summary: The terms the course uses constantly: IDP, golden path, orchestrator, IaC, GitOps, DORA, MVPlatform and more.

items: **IDP (Internal Developer Platform)**: the entire self-service infrastructure platform built for developers; the product the platform team ships
**DevEx (developer experience)**: how easy, fast and pleasant developers find their work
**Golden path**: the paved, opinionated, supported route to build, deploy and run services → reduces decision fatigue and cognitive load
**Ticket ops** (anti-pattern): devs open tickets for every infra change
**Platform Orchestrator**: the backend engine of an IDP → dynamically generates app and infra configs as a resource graph on every deployment

items.t: **IaC (Infrastructure as Code)**: treats provisioning like software → version-controlled, testable, repeatable

items: **Score**: the CNCF workload specification → platform-agnostic YAML in which developers describe what a workload needs without infra knowledge
**CDE (Cloud Development Environment)**: an automated, standardised dev environment in the cloud
**GitOps**: keeps desired application and infrastructure configuration in Git → delivery tooling reconciles running systems with that desired state

items.t: **Four DORA metrics** (as the lecture uses them):

items: **MVPlatform** (Minimum Viable Platform): the smallest platform delivering real value
**Cognitive load**: the mental effort demanded of developers
**Platform as a Product**: gives the IDP a roadmap, feedback, SLOs and an owning team
**Team Topologies** → contrasts the platform team supporting developers with application teams aligned to business streams

terms.def: Internal Developer Platform: the self-service platform that is the platform team's product.
Opinionated, supported route for building, deploying and running services.
Versioned desired configuration in Git, with delivery tooling reconciling running systems to it.
Deployment Frequency, Lead Time, MTTR, Change Failure Rate.
Minimum Viable Platform: smallest platform that delivers real value.

check.q: Six months after launch, a platform team wants to prove ROI and proposes reporting the number of portal logins per week. Does that metric show the platform's value?

items: **Logins measure activity**, not **delivery performance** → can rise simply because teams are **forced onto the portal**

items.t: **Use instead** → compare against the **baseline measured before launch**:
sub: **DORA metrics**: deployment frequency, lead time, MTTR, change failure rate

a.foot: Logins are useful only as a **secondary adoption signal**.

check.q: After a platform launch, deployment frequency rises but change failure rate also rises. Has the platform clearly improved delivery?

items: **Delivery is faster but less reliable** → the evidence is **mixed**
**Check** **lead time** and **MTTR** as well
**Look at** whether the **golden path** is missing **tests or guardrails** that teams used to apply by hand
**Developer feedback** shows whether the automation **reduces or just moves** the effort

check.q: In a GitOps setup, an engineer fixes a production configuration by editing the cluster directly. What happens next, and what should they have done?

items: **Git is the single source of truth** → the **CD tool** keeps **syncing the cluster to Git**
**Result** → overwrites the manual change, or leaves it as **unrecorded drift**
**Should have**: made the change through a **pull request** → **reviewed, versioned and reproducible**
a.foot: **GitOps trades** the speed of a direct edit for **auditability and repeatability**.

sections.title: IDP reference architecture: the planes
sections.summary: An IDP separates developer intent, delivery automation and running resources. Observability, security and AI/ML support apply across that path.

notes.lead: The reference model is layered into planes:
items: **Developer Control Plane**
**Integration and Delivery Plane**
**Resource Plane**
**Monitoring and Logging Plane** (observability)
**Security Plane**

items.t: **Data and Model Management Plane** (new in v2.0) → ML lifecycle support

notes.foot: In practice: five core planes plus this AI/ML plane.

items: **Developer portals** (Backstage, Port) → discovery, scaffolding, dashboards and docs
**Workload specifications** (Score) → say WHAT a workload needs, not HOW
**CLI tooling**
**Declarative config** (KubeVela/OAM, Helm values) → hides infra complexity
**CI pipeline** → GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI
**Image registry** → Docker Hub, ECR
**Platform orchestrator** → the intelligence layer: generates resource graphs, manages progression between environments
**CD system** → ArgoCD or Flux, syncs cluster state to Git
**Kubernetes clusters** → managed K8s dominant: EKS, AKS, GKE
**Databases** → RDS, Cloud SQL
**Storage** → S3, Blob, GCS
**DNS and networking** → service meshes such as Istio, ingress
**Cloud services** → queues, Pub/Sub, Redis, AI APIs

items.t: **Monitoring and Logging** → Prometheus, ELK, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Datadog
sub: observability collects metrics, logs, traces and SLOs from every plane

items.t: **Security** → Vault, AWS/Azure secret managers, OPA, Snyk
sub: embeds secrets, policies, RBAC, compliance and AI-agent guardrails everywhere

items: **Developer** (portal, IDE, CLI, CDE) submits a Score workload spec
**Control plane** (Backstage, workload API) passes it to the orchestrator
**Orchestrator** (platform API, resource graph) drives the resource plane (K8s, GPU, DB, cloud services)
**CD/GitOps** (ArgoCD, Flux) deploys to the environment
notes.foot: Observability, security and data/model planes are active throughout.

notes.lead: Maps the model to Singapore agencies. SHIP-HATS is a DevSecOps maturity model with seven steps:
items: **Ad hoc practice**
**Source code management**
**Continuous integration**
**Artifact management**
**Continuous delivery**
**Continuous monitoring**
**Continuous improvement**
notes.foot: SHIP-HATS provides **managed tooling for steps 2 to 5**: SaaS (GitLab) and self-hosted tools (SonarQube, Nexus) deploying into agencies' own AWS or Azure environments.

terms.def: Self-service UI (e.g. Backstage) for service discovery, scaffolding, dashboards and docs.
Dependency graph of app and infra resources generated by the orchestrator at each deployment.
Singapore government DevSecOps platform covering source management through continuous delivery.

check.q: Developers on your platform currently write raw cluster manifests and infrastructure code for every service. A teammate proposes a workload spec in the developer control plane with an orchestrator behind it. What does this buy, and what does it cost?

items: **Developers declare WHAT** a workload needs (e.g. a database or a port) **without infrastructure knowledge**
**Orchestrator decides HOW** → generates **app and infrastructure configs** as a **resource graph** on each deployment
**Buys**: lower **cognitive load**; **standards and security** consistent across teams
a.foot: **Cost**: the platform team must **build and maintain the orchestrator rules**, and developers **lose direct control** of details.

check.q: A security lead proposes one security scan as the final stage before production. Where does the reference architecture put security, and why does that matter?

items: **Security is a cross-cutting plane**, **embedded everywhere**
**Secrets management**, **identity**, **access control**, **policies** and **compliance** apply to **every plane**, not just the last step
**A single final gate** → finds problems **late** and leaves **secrets and access** in earlier stages **unmanaged**
a.foot: Embedding it costs more **platform work up front** but makes **the secure path the default**.

check.q: A developer's workload spec is accepted, but the service fails in staging because no database exists there. Using the planes, where would you look first?

items: **Orchestrator** (in the **integration and delivery plane**) → turns the spec into a **resource graph for each environment**
**Resource plane** → **provisions** what that graph asks for
**Check first**: does the **staging resource graph** include the database, and did **provisioning run**?
**Observability plane** → should give **logs from every plane**
a.foot: This shows why **cross-cutting monitoring** matters.

check.q: A data science team wants to train and deploy models through the existing IDP. What does the reference model add for them, and why is the resource plane alone not enough?

items.t: **Adds the data and model management plane**:
sub: covers the **ML lifecycle** up to **production governance**

items: **Resource plane alone** → can supply **GPU nodes**, but doesn't track which **data and experiment** produced which **model**
a.foot: Without that plane the platform can **run** ML workloads but cannot **govern** them.

visuals.title: Intent becomes a running workload

steps.label: Describe workload
steps.detail: A portal, CLI or Score specification expresses what the application needs without prescribing infrastructure.

steps.label: Build and configure
steps.detail: CI builds and tests artifacts. The orchestrator generates application and infrastructure configuration.

steps.label: Provision and deploy
steps.detail: Provision clusters, databases and other dependencies; CD deploys the application to its environment.

visuals.caption: Observability and security apply across every step; the data and model plane supports AI/ML workloads across the same path.

sections.title: Adoption, trends and the platform journey
sections.summary: Why organisations adopt platform engineering, where they are on maturity, where the discipline is heading (shifting down, AI) and the five-step journey to a mature IDP.

items: **Missing automation** → 49%
**Inconsistent DevOps setups** → 48%
**Cognitive overload** → 47%
**Ticket ops** → 44%
**Also matter**: security gaps, delivery speed, onboarding
**Maturity**: most teams are in the Operational band; measurement is weakest, with 43% still provisional
**Shift down** → put repeatable infrastructure, security, compliance, observability and cost controls into platform automation
**Shift left** → moves checks earlier in delivery
notes.foot: Shifting down supplies the shared capability so earlier checks do not become extra manual work for each developer.

items.t: **AI-powered platforms** (platform teams build):
**Platforms for AI**:

notes.foot: **94%** of organisations see AI as critical or important to platform engineering's future.

items.t: **Artisan model** (replaced):
**Industrial model**:
**Grab super-app** illustrates → one platform growing many services on shared foundations
sub: ride-hailing, food, grocery, payments, logistics, financial services

items: **Identify pain** and its cost
**Define the smallest useful platform**
**Build automation** → provisioning, CI/CD and IaC
**Add interfaces** → portal or CLI
**Measure and expand**
notes.foot: The final step does not mean waiting to measure: establish delivery and satisfaction baselines from day one.

terms.def: Embedding toil (security, compliance, reliability) into the platform instead of pushing it onto developers.
Net promoter score from developers, used to measure platform satisfaction and prove value.
Platform teams both use AI to improve the platform and build platforms for AI workloads.

check.q: A platform team's first deliverable is a polished developer portal, while provisioning behind it is still done by ticket. Do you support the plan?

items: **Backend before portal** (the lecture's principle): a portal is **only an interface**
**Ticket-driven provisioning behind it** → nothing **self-service** happens
**Build first** the automation for the **top pain**: typically **CI/CD and IaC**, **golden paths** and an **orchestrator**
**Then** put a **portal or CLI** on top
a.foot: A portal can come early only as a **thin front** for automation that **already works**.

check.q: A security lead wants every developer to run three extra scanning tools by hand before each merge. Is this shifting left or shifting down, and what would you suggest?

items: **Shifting left**: moves checks **earlier** but **dumps the toil on developers**
**Shifting down**: embed the scans in the platform as **automated guardrails** and **secure defaults** on the **golden path** → the **safe route is also the easiest**
a.foot: The checks can still run early; what changes is **who does the work**.

check.q: A platform team plans an 18-month build covering every plane before any application team uses it. What would you change?

a.lead: Start with a **minimum viable platform** that solves the **most costly pain**, then expand.
items: **Long build with no users** → **delays value** and gets **no feedback** → the team may **build the wrong things**
Goes against the **'treat it as a product'** principle
**Measure from day one** → each step's impact is visible

check.q: A maturity survey shows most organisations stuck at 'Operational', with measurement the weakest dimension. Your new platform team has no baseline numbers. What do you do first, and why?

items: **Do first**: document the **current cost of the pain** (e.g. **ticket wait times**, **lead time**, **failure rates**) **before building anything**
**Why**: a platform is a **product that must prove ROI**
**No baseline** → no later **DORA** or **NPS** figure can show improvement
a.foot: Cheap to do **at the start**; almost **impossible to reconstruct later**.

steps.label: Identify pain
steps.detail: Ticket ops, cognitive overload and no standards are the starting problems; record their cost to justify the platform.

steps.label: Define MVP
steps.detail: Build the smallest platform that solves the top pain, starting with CI/CD and IaC rather than a portal.

steps.label: Build backend
steps.detail: Automate provisioning and create golden paths using an orchestrator or pipelines.

steps.label: Add interfaces
steps.detail: Put a portal and CLI on top so developers self-serve common workflows.

steps.label: Measure and grow
steps.detail: Compare DORA metrics and developer NPS with the baseline collected from day one, then expand where evidence shows value.

sections.title: Platform thinking: the network business model
sections.summary: A platform as a business that enables interactions between producers and consumers, and the three components (Magnet, Toolbox, Matchmaker) that make it work and scale.

items: **Where value is made**: platforms are where users create and exchange value in an ecosystem
**Definition**: infrastructure that enables interactions between **Producers** and **Consumers** via information (the **Seed**)
**Think roles, not markets** → the same person can be a consumer and a producer
**Linear (pipeline)** → focuses on process: production, assembly, distribution
**Network** → focuses on interactions between producers and consumers through the platform
**Disrupted by platforms of this kind** → accommodation, transportation, telecommunication, news, computing

notes.lead: Identify the seed, producer, consumer and exchange before selecting technology.

items.t: **YouTube** worked application:

items: **Same person** can occupy both roles
**Get both roles** onto the platform
**Convert consumers into producers** over time → saves marketing spend
**Get producers to produce more seeds** → scales production
**Tools that enable interaction** → let producers create and consumers consume
**Well-designed APIs**
**Remove barriers**
**Co-design principle**
**Get external parties to contribute**
**Accurate matching** → minimise false positives
**Curation** → separates high- and low-quality seeds (voting, ratings)
**Trust mechanisms**
**Machine learning**

items.t: **Build one interaction at a time** → LinkedIn:
sub: professional to professional first → for adoption
then recruiters and job seekers → for monetisation

items.t: **Decide who moderates content**:

terms.def: The unit of value or information (e.g. a video, listing) that producers create and consumers seek.
Component that attracts and retains producers and consumers.
Tools, APIs and SDKs that let producers create and consumers consume value.
Component that matches, curates and builds trust, using data analytics and ML.
Business centred on interactions between roles rather than a linear production process.

check.q: A video site runs separate marketing budgets for creators and for viewers, treating them as two markets. What does 'think roles not markets' suggest instead?

items: **Users can play both roles** → viewers can become creators
**Magnet strategy** → converts **consumers into producers** over time
**Benefit** → saves **marketing spend** and **scales production of seeds**
a.foot: So invest in **lowering the barrier to producing** (e.g. **simple upload tools**) rather than buying **two separate audiences**.

check.q: A tutoring marketplace has plenty of registered tutors, but students complain that matches are poor and some tutors are low quality. Which platform component is weak, and what would you build?

a.lead: The **matchmaker**, not the magnet: supply exists, but **matching and curation** fail.
items: **Matching accuracy** → improve it to cut **false positives**
**Curate** tutors using **ratings and reviews**
**Trust mechanisms**
**ML** applied to matching
a.foot: In engineering terms: **curation components** and **matching algorithms**.

check.q: A furniture maker sells only its own products through its web shop and calls itself a platform because the shop has a public API. Is this a linear or a network business?

items: **Linear** → focus is the **process of production, assembly and distribution** of its **own goods**
**Network business** → focuses on **enabling interactions** between **independent producers and consumers**
**Technology is only an enabler** (lecture) → an **API alone does not make a platform**
a.foot: It would move towards a **network model** if **other makers** could list and sell through it.

check.q: A start-up wants to launch professional networking, messaging, job listings and content publishing all at once. What does the LinkedIn example advise?

items.t: **LinkedIn** started with **professional-to-professional connections**, each step **building adoption before monetisation**:

items: **Launching everything at once** → spreads the **magnet** thin → **too few producers** for any single interaction

center.label: Platform
center.detail: Starts from one seed and the producer and consumer roles; technology is only an enabler of the interaction.

items.label: Magnet
items.detail: Get both roles on board, convert consumers to producers over time and get producers to create more seeds.

items.label: Toolbox
items.detail: Tools that let producers create and consumers consume; design the right APIs, remove barriers, co-design and let external parties contribute.

items.label: Matchmaker
items.detail: Accurate matching with few false positives, curation of high- versus low-quality seeds, trust mechanisms and ML, driven by data analytics.

sections.title: Business ecosystems and the engineering perspective
sections.summary: Platforms as enablers of business ecosystems, and how each platform-business aspect translates into an engineering concern.

items: **Platform ecosystem** → composed of externally produced complements that augment the platform
**Platform + all apps** interoperating through its interfaces together form its ecosystem

items.t: **Business ecosystem** → the wider network of organisations involved in delivering a product or service, through both competition and cooperation

items: **Choose functionality and technology** → to help producers and consumers exchange value
**A feature is useful** when it improves that exchange or the ecosystem around it
**Seed** → domain entities
**Producers and consumers** → domain entities, scalability and performance
**Interactions** → service design, architecting and exposing services, business process, scalability, performance
**Magnet** → service usability design, incentive components, data analytics components
**Toolbox** → service usability, SDK design, API design, integration with other services
**Matchmaker** → curation components and algorithms
**Scaling the business** → modular, extensible components and agile architecture
**Ecosystem** → architecting for availability, security and scalability
**Provide** composable components, services and infrastructure → to build and host applications
**Enable** business ecosystems
**Provide** extensibility, innovation and co-creation
**Include** data analytics → to improve the business
notes.foot: **Platform thinking** is needed to engineer a platform as a business.

terms.def: The platform plus the externally produced complements that interoperate through its interfaces.
Network of suppliers, distributors, customers, competitors and agencies delivering a product through competition and cooperation.

check.q: Partners praise a platform's matching algorithm but say its SDK is confusing and integration takes weeks. Which platform aspect is weak, and which engineering concerns does it map to?

items: **Toolbox** = the **tools producers and consumers use to interact**
**Engineering concerns**: **service usability design**, **SDK and API design**, **integration with other services**
a.foot: A strong **matchmaker** cannot make up for a toolbox that **keeps partners from joining**.

check.q: Hundreds of third-party apps now depend on a platform's interfaces. A product manager proposes putting all of this quarter's effort into new features and deferring availability and security work. Do you agree?

items: **Architecting for the ecosystem** = **availability**, **security** and **scalability**
**Why** → an **outage or breach** now hits **every complement** built on the platform, not just one app
**Features still matter** for **growth**
a.foot: So the answer depends on whether **current availability and security** already meet **partners' needs**.

check.q: A platform plans to add a new kind of interaction every quarter, as the sample paper's ecosystem-growth question describes. Which engineering aspect must the design support, and what goes wrong without it?

items: **Needs** → **modular, extensible components** and an **agile architecture** for **scaling the platform business**
**Each new interaction** → plugs in as **new services** that **reuse existing domain entities and interfaces**
**Without it** → every addition means **changing the core** → each release **slows down** and risks **breaking existing interactions**

exam_angles.q: A food-delivery company wants to open its ordering, delivery-tracking and payment capabilities to independent restaurants and couriers. (a) Identify the seed, producers, consumers and core interaction. (b) The CEO wants to launch restaurant booking, grocery delivery and a courier marketplace in the same release. Advise. (c) Give two engineering concerns that follow from opening the APIs to outside parties.

items.t: **(a) Roles**
sub: **Interaction**: browse, order, match a courier, deliver, pay

items.t: **(b) Build one interaction at a time**, as **LinkedIn** did
sub: Get **food ordering** adopted and **growing producers** through the **magnet** before adding new interactions
Design **modular, extensible components** so later ones **plug in**

items.t: **(c) Engineering concerns**
sub: **Many outside parties** now depend on the platform → architect for **availability**, **security** and **scalability**

a.foot: **Trade-off**: slower initial scope in exchange for a **stable core**.

exam_angles.q: A company with 40 application teams has a five-day ticket wait for databases, each team maintains its own pipeline scripts, and leadership wants evidence of value within six months. Propose the first steps of an IDP, the measures you would use, and one thing you would deliberately not build first.

items.t: **Baseline first**: document the **cost of the pain**
**Minimum viable platform** aimed at the **top pain**
**Measures**: **DORA metrics** and **developer NPS** against the baseline
**Don't build first**: a full **developer portal**
sub: a portal over **ticket-driven provisioning** would show nothing in **six months**

exam_angles.q: On an IDP, developers submit workload specs. Staging deployments work, but production sometimes gets a different database size and nobody can explain why. Using the reference architecture and GitOps, diagnose where to look and what to change.

items.t: **Look at the orchestrator** (**integration and delivery plane**)
sub: it generates **environment-specific configuration** as a **resource graph**
→ compare the **production and staging graphs** and the **rules** that produce them

items.t: **Check GitOps**: was production state **changed outside Git**?
sub: **Git** should be the **single source of truth**
every **infra change** should go through a **reviewed PR**

items: **Fix**: move **environment differences** into **versioned config** and let **CD sync from Git**
**Observability plane** → should **record what was deployed**, so the next difference is visible without detective work

exam_angles.q: An organisation with 300 developers has a DevOps culture and an SRE team that owns SLOs and error budgets, but onboarding a new service still takes three weeks. The CIO asks whether to grow the SRE team or create a platform team. Advise, and say what would change your answer.

items: **Symptom** = **slow onboarding** and **missing self-service** → these are **platform engineering's** concerns
**Platform team offers**: **golden paths**, **standardised provisioning**, **lower cognitive load**, with **developers treated as customers**
**SRE keeps owning reliability**; the platform can make **SLO monitoring a default** for every new service
a.foot: **What would change it**: if the main problem were **frequent outages** or **missed SLOs** instead of slow onboarding → **growing SRE** would be the better answer.

exam_angles.q: A regulated firm requires secret scanning, dependency checks and policy checks for every service. Option A gives each team a checklist to run before release. Option B builds the checks into the platform's golden path. Choose one and give the trade-off.

items.t: **Option B = shifting down**: checks embedded as **automated guardrails** and **secure defaults**
sub: makes the **compliant path the easiest** one

items.t: **Option A = shifting left**: checks happen **early**, but

a.foot: **Trade-off**: B costs **platform investment up front**, and teams that **leave the golden path** still need a way to **show compliance**.

exam_angles.q: A bank's architecture group plans to give its teams (a) a shared code skeleton with abstract classes, (b) a utility code package for date and currency handling, and (c) a hosted environment exposing identity and payment services through APIs, which partners may also use. Classify each, and explain which one creates an ecosystem and what that obliges the bank to do.

items: **(a) Framework**: teams use it and it **dictates structure**
**(b) Library**: teams **call it where they choose**
**(c) Platform**: **hosted**, **accessed by APIs**, and **extensible by outside parties**

items.t: **Ecosystem: only (c)** → partners can build **complementary products** through its interfaces
sub: **Obliges the bank** to keep those **interfaces stable** so **internal change does not break partners**
**Obliges the bank** to architect for **availability**, **security** and **scalability**
